children.text: To take in heat within the system in an endothermic process.
How closely a measurement aligns with a correct value.
A weak acid or base that changes color when it goes from its acidic to its basic form.
A reaction involving the transfer of a hydrogen ion between reactant species.
A reaction involving the transfer of a proton from an acid to water, yielding hydronium ions and the conjugate base of the acid.
The equilibrium constant for an acid-ionization reaction. Also called
Actinium and the elements in the second row or the f-block, atomic numbers 89–103. Also called
A temporary unstable collection of atoms that exists briefly before products are formed during a chemical reaction.
The minimum amount of energy required for reactants to reach the transition state and proceed with the reaction.
The minimum energy molecules need to react; the height of the energy barrier to formation of products.
An electrode that participates as a reactant or product in the redox reaction of an electrochemical cell; the mass of an active electrode changes during the redox reaction.
Amount of product formed in a reaction.
The force of attraction between two different molecules.
A process in which atoms, molecules, or ions of a liquid, gas, or dissolved solid adhere to a surface.

A primary battery similar to a dry cell that uses an alkaline (often potassium hydroxide) electrolyte; designed to be an improved replacement for the dry cell but with more energy storage and less electrolyte leakage than the typical dry cell.
Element that exists in the same physical state but in different forms because of differences in the way its atoms are bonded.

A type of radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle (consisting of two protons and two neutrons) and transforms into a new nucleus with a lower atomic number and mass number.
A high-energy helium nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons, resulting from the loss of two electrons from a helium atom. It is commonly emitted during radioactive decay processes.
The pressure on an object that comes from its surroundings, such as from a gas or liquid in contact with the object.
A solid in which the particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) lack an ordered internal structure. Also called
Of, relating to, or being a compound consisting of molecules having a polar water-soluble group attached to a water-insoluble hydrocarbon chain.
Describes species that may either donate or accept a proton.
Describes species that can act as either an acid or a base.
The magnitude of the wave's displacement—half the distance between the crests and troughs.
A chemical species of interest in an analysis.
Quantum number distinguishing the different shapes of orbitals; it is also a measure of the orbital angular momentum.
The electrode in an electrochemical cell where oxidation occurs; the site where electrons are released (from which electrons flow away).
A molecular orbital in which electron density is decreased in the region between the two nuclei. Electrons in an antibonding orbital destabilize the molecule.
A solution for which water is the solvent.
The smallest building block of nature; the smallest particle of an element.
Average mass of atoms of an element, expressed in atomic mass units (amu).
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, represented by
Mathematical function that describes the properties of an electron in an atom.
The theory that all matter is composed of minute particles called atoms.

Procedure in which the electron configuration of the elements is determined by “building” them in order of atomic numbers, adding one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the proper subshell at a time.
The process in which water spontaneously produces low concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions through the transfer of protons between water molecules.
The volume of a gas at constant temperature and pressure is proportional to the number of gas molecules.
Defined value of the number of entities comprising 1 mole of substance, equal to 6.022 × 10
A balance measures mass by comparing an unknown mass to a known mass. This measurement is not affected by changes in gravity.
A chemical reaction equation with equal numbers of atoms for each element in the reactants and products.
A representation that shows the geometric arrangement of the atoms of a given substance with atomic sizes not to scale.
Region on a graph of proton number versus neutron number containing all the stable (nonradioactive) nuclides. Also called the
A reaction involving the transfer of a proton from water to a base, yielding hydroxide ions and the conjugate acid of the base.
The equilibrium constant for a base-ionization reaction. Also called
SI unit of radioactivity; 1 Bq represents a rate of radioactive decay equal to 1 disintegration/s.

A type of radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus transforms by emitting a beta particle. Beta decay results in the change of the atomic number of the nucleus without a significant change in its mass number.
A ligand that coordinates to one central metal through coordinate bonds from two different atoms.
An elementary step involving two reactant species.
Ionic compound consisting of a monatomic cation and a monatomic anion.
A blackbody is an idealized perfect absorber of all incident electromagnetic radiation; such bodies emit electromagnetic radiation in characteristic continuous spectra called blackbody radiation.
Describes a unit cell that contains two atoms: one-eighth of an atom at each of its eight corners plus one atom in the center.
The increase in boiling point observed when nonvolatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, Δ
The temperature at which a liquid's equilibrium vapor pressure is equal to the pressure exerted on the liquid by its gaseous surroundings.
A device designed to measure the energy change for processes occurring under conditions of constant volume; commonly used for reactions involving solid and gaseous reactants or products.
The angle between any two bonds that include a common atom, usually measured in degrees.
Separation of charge in a bond that depends on the difference in electronegativity and the bond distance represented by partial charges or a vector.
The distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms along the straight line joining the nuclei. Also called
The energy required to break a specific covalent bond in one mole of gaseous molecules.
In Lewis structures: The number of electron pairs per bound atom pair. In molecular orbital (MO) theory: The number of electrons in bonding MOs minus the number in antibonding MOs, multiplied by ½.
A molecular orbital in which electron density is increased in the region between the two nuclei. Electrons in a bonding orbital stabilize the molecule.
The volume of a given number of moles of gas held at constant temperature is inversely proportional to the pressure under which it is measured.
A substance that donates a proton.
A substance that accepts a proton.
A mixture of appreciable amounts of a weak acid–base pair; the pH of a buffer resists change when small amounts of acid or base are added.
A device used for the precise delivery of variable liquid volumes, such as in a titration analysis.
A unit of heat or other energy; the amount of energy required to raise 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius; 1 cal is defined as 4.184 J.
A device used to measure the amount of heat absorbed or released in a chemical or physical process.
The process of measuring the amount of heat involved in a chemical or physical process.
The flow of a liquid through a porous material or narrow space without the assistance of, or in opposition to, gravity.
The increase in rate of a chemical reaction due to the addition of a catalyst.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed by the reaction.
The electrode in an electrochemical cell where reduction occurs; the site where electrons are gained (to which electrons flow toward).
An approach to preventing corrosion of a metal object by connecting it to a sacrificial anode composed of a more readily oxidized metal.
A symbolic representation of the components and reactions in an electrochemical cell. Also called
The measure of the voltage (electrical potential difference) between the two electrodes of an electrochemical cell; indicates the cell's ability to produce an electric current.
An ion or atom to which one or more ligands is attached through coordinate covalent bonds.
Partial positive charge on one atom and partial negative on another; occurs when bonding electrons are concentrated closer to one atom than the other.
The volume of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the pressure is held constant.
A complex formed from a polydentate ligand attached to a central metal.
A ligand that attaches to a central metal ion by bonds from two or more donor atoms.
A force or attraction that holds atoms together to form a molecule.
A change in matter that always produces one or more types of matter that differ from the matter present before the change.
The identities of the substances contained in the matter.
The variation in the chemical composition, structure, or properties between two substances.
A symbolic representation of a chemical reaction.
Chemical identity is the answer to the question, What type of matter is it?
Characteristics of a substance, such as flammability and reactivity, that can be seen during a chemical reaction. A substance's inability to change is also considered a chemical property.
A set of chemically identical molecular entities.
The study of the composition, properties, and interactions of matter.
A medical treatment similar to internal radiation therapy, but chemical rather than radioactive substances are introduced into the body to kill cancer cells.
Configuration of a geometrical isomer in which two similar groups are on the same side of an imaginary reference line on the molecule.
The mathematical relationship between the temperature, vapor pressure, and enthalpy of vaporization for a substance.
The process of two or more substances pulling together to form a larger mass.
Numbers placed in front of symbols or formulas in a chemical equation to indicate their relative amounts.
The force of attraction between two identical molecules.
Properties of a solution that depend only on the concentration of solute particles.

A model describing how reactions take place at the molecular level that emphasizes the kinetic energy and orientation molecules have when they collide with each other and the rate at which the collisions take place.
A mixture in which particles are substantially larger than ordinary molecules but small enough that they do not settle out.
A range in pH over which the color change of an indicator is observed.
For a fixed amount of gas, the ratio of the product of pressure and volume to the absolute temperature is constant.
A gravimetric technique used to determine the elemental composition of a compound via the collection and weighing of its gaseous combustion products.
Vigorous redox reaction producing significant amounts of energy in the form of heat and, sometimes, light.

The effect on an existing equilibrium when a substance containing an ion in common with the dissolved species is added to the solution; causes a decrease in the solubility of an ionic species or a decrease in the ionization of a weak acid or base.
An equation in which all dissolved ions are explicitly expressed.
An ion consisting of a central (usually transition metal) atom or ion surrounded by molecules or ions, called ligands, often via coordinate covalent bonds.
What the matter is made of.
A pure substance that can be broken down into simpler substances by chemical changes.
A qualitative term for a solution containing solute at a relatively high concentration.
A quantitative measure of the relative amounts of solute and solvent present in a solution.

An electrochemical cell in which both half-cells consist of the same substances, but the solutions have different concentrations; it has a potential difference and produces current due to the concentration gradient.
A change in concentration from one region to another.
The transition of a substance from the gaseous (vapor) phase to the liquid phase.
An abbreviated way to write electron configurations by replacing the core electron configuration with the matching noble gas symbol and retaining the valence electrons.
Able to transfer heat or energy.
Substance formed when a base gains a proton.
An acid and a base that differ only by the presence or absence of a proton (H
Substance formed when an acid loses a proton.
An acid–base pair in which the two substances differ by only one proton.
A pure substance always contains the same elements in the same proportions.
The result of two in-phase waves combining, which increases the amplitude of the wave.

A three-part structure of materials that protects the exterior of a nuclear fission reactor and operating personnel from the high temperatures, pressures, and radiation levels inside the reactor. Also called a
Electromagnetic radiation given off in an unbroken series of wavelengths (e.g., white light from the sun).
Material inserted into the fuel assembly that absorbs neutrons and can be raised or lowered to adjust the rate of a fission reaction.
A covalent bond in which both electrons originated from the same atom. Also called

A stable substance consisting of a central metal atom or ion (acting as a Lewis acid) surrounded by molecules or ions (ligands) that donate pairs of electrons (acting as Lewis bases) through coordinate covalent bonds.
The number of coordinate covalent bonds to the central metal atom in a complex or the number of closest contacts to an atom in a crystalline form.
The central metal atom or ion plus the attached ligands of a complex.
Electrons occupying the inner shell of an atom.
Degradation of metal via a natural electrochemical process.
An experimental law describing the force between two electrically charged particles at rest.
An ion of opposite charge that accompanies a charged species in a compound to maintain electrical neutrality; it balances the charge of complex ions within a coordination compound.
A system characterized by the simultaneous establishment of two or more equilibrium reactions with one or more shared substances.
Bond formed when electrons are shared between atoms.
Molecule formed by covalent bonds, which are chemical bonds that share rather than transfer electrons.
A substance whose atoms are bonded by covalent bonds in a continuous network throughout the material.
One-half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms when they are joined by a covalent bond.
Substance whose molecules are formed by covalent bonds, which are chemical bonds that share rather than transfer electrons.

The minimum amount of fissile material needed to maintain a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Below this mass, the chain reaction will not be sustained, and above it, the reaction can increase exponentially.
The end point of a phase equilibrium curve; the highest temperature and pressure at which two phases of a substance (e.g., liquid and gas) can coexist.
orbitals due to differences in their interactions with ligands.
A model that explains the energies of the orbitals in transition metals in terms of electrostatic interactions with the ligands but does not include metal ligand bonding.
A description of the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, ions, or molecules inside a crystalline solid.
A solid whose structure consists of particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) in a highly ordered, regular pattern.
Describes a unit cell that has three repeating layers of hexagonally arranged atoms.
A  unit for rate of radioactive decay frequently used in medicine; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10
The total pressure of a mixture of ideal gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the component gases.
The nuclide that is produced as a result of the radioactive decay of a parent nuclide. It may itself be stable or may undergo further radioactive decay.
Elements in groups 3 through 11 with valence electrons in
A chemical reaction in which one reactant breaks apart down into two or more products.
Orbitals that have the same energy levels.
Ratio of mass to volume for a substance or object.

The number of donor atoms in a ligand that directly bind to a central metal atom or ion in a coordination complex. It indicates how many points of attachment the ligand has to the metal (monodentate, bidentate, etc.) based on the number of coordinating atoms.
A process in which a gaseous substance condenses directly into the solid state, bypassing the liquid state.
The result of two out-of-phase waves combining, which decreases amplitude as the waves cancel each other out.

Describes substances that are repelled by an external magnetic field due to the absence of unpaired electrons. Diamagnetic materials create an induced magnetic field in a direction opposite to the applied magnetic field and do not have a net magnetic moment.
Phenomenon in which a material is not magnetic itself but is repelled by a magnetic field; occurs when only paired electrons are present.
A molecule made up of only two atoms.
The change in the direction of travel experienced by an electromagnetic wave when it encounters a physical barrier whose dimensions are comparable to those of the wavelength of the light.
A surface with identical, regularly spaced elements used to separate (diffract) light into individual wavelengths and produce a spectrum.
The movement of atoms or molecules from a region of relatively high concentration to one of relatively low concentration.
A qualitative term for a solution containing solute at a relatively low concentration.
The process of adding solvent to a solution in order to lower the concentration of solutes.
Method used to convert from one unit of measure to another.
The process of joining two identical or similar molecular entities by bonds.
A pair of equal but opposite charges (one positive, one negative) on a molecule.
Property of a molecule that describes the separation of charge determined by the sum of the individual bond moments based on the molecular structure.
The electrostatic force between the partially positive end of one polar molecule and the partially negative end of another.
An acid that has two ionizable hydrogen atoms per molecule.
A base that will accept two protons.
As one variable increases, another variable increases at the same rate, and vice versa.
The substance present as relatively large solid or liquid particles in a colloid (the solute).
The attractive force between in instantaneous dipoles in adjacent molecules or atoms. Also called
A solid, liquid, or gas in which colloidal particles are dispersed.
General process in which one particle separates into smaller particles, usually in a reversible manner.
The physical process accompanying the dissolution of an ionic compound in which the compound’s constituent ions are solvated and dispersed throughout the solution.
Equilibrium constant for the decomposition of a complex ion into its components; it is the inverse of the formations constant (
An atom in a ligand with a lone pair of electrons that forms a coordinate covalent bond to a central metal.
A bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.
A primary battery, also called a
, based on the spontaneous oxidation of zinc by manganese(IV).
The capacity of a material to be stretched, such as into a wire, without losing strength or breaking.
The status of a system in which reciprocal processes, such as vaporization and condensation, occur at equal rates.
The pull exerted on a specific electron by the nucleus, taking into account any electron–electron repulsions.
The escape of gaseous atoms or molecules through a tiny hole in a container into a vacuum.
The physical property of matter that causes it to experience a force when in an electromagnetic field. Charge can be positive or negative; like charges repel and unlike charges attract each other.
A flow of charged particles that move through a material or space; the net rate of flow of electric charge through a surface.
The amount of energy needed to move a unit charge from a reference point to a specific point in an electric field.
Energy a charged particle has because of its position relative to other charged particles.
A device that generates electrical energy from spontaneous chemical reactions (galvanic cells) or uses electrical energy to drive nonspontaneous reactions (electrolytic cells).
A conductor through which electricity enters or leaves an electrochemical cell; the anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs, and the cathode, where reduction occurs.
The potential of a cell in which the half-cell of interest acts as a cathode when connected to the standard hydrogen electrode.
A process using electrical energy to cause a nonspontaneous process to occur.
Substance that yields ions when dissolved in aqueous solution.
An electrochemical cell in which an external source of electrical power is used to drive an otherwise nonspontaneous process.
Energy change associated with addition of an electron to a gaseous atom or ion.

A process in which an unstable nucleus captures an inner orbital electron and combines it with a proton to form a neutron and a neutrino. This decreases the atomic number by 1 without changing the mass number, often leaving the daughter nuclide in an excited state.
The region of negative charge around an atom's nucleus that is associated with the atom's orbitals. Also called a
Listing that identifies the electron occupancy of an atom’s shells and subshells.
A representation of the probability of finding an electron in a specific location around an atom or molecule.
Molecule or ion with too few valence electrons to follow the octet rule.
Electron pair repulsion is the principle that electron pairs repel each other and position themselves as far apart as possible.
Geometric arrangement around a central atom of all regions of electron density (bonds, lone pairs, or unpaired electrons).
The tendency of an atom to attract electrons in a bond to itself.
Forces of attraction or repulsion between particles caused by their electric charges or fields.
One step in a series of simple reactions that show the progress of a reaction at the molecular level. Also called
Pure substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical changes.
Formula showing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms present in a compound.
The sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms represented in an empirical formula.
An amphiphilic substance used to stabilize the particles of some emulsions.
A colloid formed from immiscible liquids.
The measured volume of titrant solution corresponding to a visible or measured change at the equivalence point (for example, the color change of an indicator).
A chemical process in which there is a net increase in free energy; Δ
is positive and the process is nonspontaneous.
A chemical reaction or physical change that absorbs heat.
Capacity to supply heat or do work.
Thermodynamic quantity representing the total heat content of a system; the sum of the internal energy and the product of pressure and volume.
The heat released or absorbed by a system under constant pressure during a chemical or physical process.

A state function that describes the dispersal of matter and energy within a system, determined by the number of possible microstates; it quantifies the system's degree of randomness and distribution of energy.
A dynamic process in which the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant and the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
The value of the reaction quotient (
) when a system is at equilibrium, representing the ratio of the concentrations (
) of the products to reactants, each raised to the power of their respective stoichiometric coefficients.
The pressure exerted by a vapor in equilibrium with a liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.

The point in a titration at which the added solute completely reacts with the solute in the initial solution. (In an acid–base reaction, the point at which the number of moles of acid is stoichiometrically equal to the number of moles of base.)
To give off heat to the surroundings in an exothermic process.
A reactant present in an amount greater than required by the reaction stoichiometry, some of which will therefore not react.
State having an energy greater than the ground-state energy.
A chemical process in which there is a net decrease in free energy; Δ
is negative and the process is spontaneous.
A chemical reaction or physical change that releases heat.
A property whose value is proportional to the amount of the substance.
Describes a unit cell that contains four atoms: one-eighth of an atom at each of its eight corners and one-half of an atom on each of its six faces.
The charge on 1 mol of electrons; F = 96,485 C/mol e−.
Elements with atomic numbers 58–71 or 90–103 that have valence electrons in
orbitals; they are frequently shown offset below the periodic table. Also called
Amount of energy required to remove the most loosely bound atom from a gaseous atom in its ground state.
A formulation of the law of conservation of energy; the internal energy of a system changes due to heat flow in or out of the system and work done on or by the system.
Transition elements in the fourth period of the periodic table (first row of the
Describes a material that can sustain a nuclear fission chain reaction when struck by a thermal (slow) neutron. Common fissile materials include uranium-235, plutonium-239, and uranium-233.

A nuclear reaction in which a heavy atomic nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, along with the release of a large amount of energy, neutrons, and gamma radiation. This process is commonly used in nuclear reactors and atomic bombs.
The ratio of the element's masses within a molecule does not change—it is constant.
Hypothetical charge assigned to an atom in a molecule, assuming the bonding electrons are shared equally between atoms.
Equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion from its components. Also called
Sum of the average masses for all atoms represented in a chemical formula; for covalent compounds, this is also the molecular mass.
Transition elements in the seventh period of the periodic table (fourth row of the
An element in the free state is not combined with or chemically bonded to any other element.
An atom, molecule, or ion that has at least one unpaired valence electron.
The transition of a substance from the liquid phase to the solid phase.
The decrease in freezing point of a dilute solution compared to that of the pure solvent, Δ
The rate of oscillation—how many wave cycles pass a stationary point per second.
A proportionality constant in the Arrhenius equation related to the frequency of favorably oriented collisions.
A device similar to a galvanic cell that requires a continuous feed of redox reactants. Also called
The combination of very light nuclei into heavier nuclei, accompanied by the conversion of mass into large amounts of energy.
A nuclear reactor in which fusion reactions of light nuclei are controlled.
An electrochemical cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction takes place. Also called
A method of protecting iron or similar metals from corrosion by coating with a thin layer of more easily oxidized zinc.

A type of radioactive decay in which an excited nucleus releases excess energy in the form of gamma rays, which are high-energy photons. This process does not change the atomic number or mass number of the nucleus but brings the nucleus to a lower energy state. Gamma emission often accompanies other forms of decay, such as alpha or beta decay.
A short wavelength, high-energy electromagnetic radiation that exhibits wave-particle duality.
The pressure of a given number of moles of gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature when the volume is held constant.
An instrument that detects and measures radiation via the ionization produced in a Geiger-Müller tube.
A colloidal dispersion of a liquid phase throughout a solid phase.
Isomers that differ in the way in which atoms are oriented in space relative to each other, leading to different physical and chemical properties.
A thermodynamic property defined in terms of a system's enthalpy, entropy, and temperature; all spontaneous processes involve a decrease in
A transparent tube with a scale marked in milliliters (mL) on the outside, used for measuring volume.
The rate of effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass of its particles.
A process in which a sample is subjected to some treatment that causes a change in the physical state of the analyte that permits its separation from the other components of the sample.
SI unit for measuring ionizing radiation dose; 1 Gy corresponds to 1 J of energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue.
State in which the electrons in an atom, ion, or molecule have the lowest energy possible. Also called
In a multistep calculation, one or more guard digits are retained (are not rounded off) until the last step of the calculation to reduce the amount of error when the final result is rounded off.
A part of an electrochemical cell where either the oxidation or reduction half-reaction occurs; it contains the redox conjugate pair (“couple”) of a single reactant.

The time required for half of the nuclei in a sample of a radioactive substance to undergo decay, reducing the number of radioactive atoms by half. It is a measure of the rate at which a radioactive substance transforms into a more stable form.
Time required for the concentration or amount of a substance to reduce to half its initial value.
Either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction.

A technique used to balance oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions by separating the overall reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balancing each separately, then combining the half-reactions to form the balanced overall redox reaction equation.
The transfer of thermal energy between two bodies.
An extensive property of a body of matter that represents the quantity of heat required to increase its temperature by 1 degree Celsius (or 1 kelvin).
A graph of the correlation between the heat added to a substance and the temperature of the substance.
It is fundamentally impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the position and the momentum of a particle.
A logarithmic version of the acid ionization constant expression, conveniently formatted for calculating the pH of buffer solutions.
If a process can be written as the sum of several stepwise processes, the enthalpy change of the total process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the various steps.
Describes a sample of matter that looks like it has different sections that have different stuff in them when looking at the matter at a particular scale.
A catalyst present in a different phase from the reactants, furnishing a surface at which a reaction can occur.
Equilibria established between substances in two or more phases, such as a gas and a liquid.
A mixture with a composition that varies from point to point and therefore has visibly different parts.
Describes molecules containing atoms of two or more elements.
Describes a unit cell that has two repeating layers of hexagonally arranged atoms.
A complex in which the electrons maximize the total electron spin by singly populating all of the orbitals before pairing two electrons into the lower-energy orbitals.
Describes a sample of matter that looks the same everywhere when looking at the matter at a particular scale.
A catalyst present in the same phase as the reactants.
Equilibria established between substances that are all in the same phase.
A mixture that has a uniform composition and appears visually the same throughout.
Describes molecules containing atoms of only one element.
Molecules consisting of only two identical atoms.
Every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied, and all electrons in singly occupied orbitals have the same spin.
An orbital that results from the mixing of different kinds of atomic orbitals on the same atom.
The mixing of different types of atomic orbitals to produce new ones whose spatial orientations match the observed molecular shapes.
Compound containing one or more water molecules bound within its crystals.
The exceptionally strong dipole-dipole attraction that exists when hydrogen is bonded to one of the three most electronegative elements: F, O, or N.
A chemical reaction in which a molecule of water breaks one or more chemical bonds.
Pressure resulting from gravity force acting on all the particles within a fluid.
The precipitation of solids from hot mineral-laden water (hydrothermal solution).
Molecule or ion containing at least one main group element that has more than eight electrons in its valence shell.
Describes a solution whose concentration of solutes is lower than that of another solution across a semipermeable membrane.
A useful way to organize initial, change, and equilibrium (ICE) data when solving equilibrium problems. Also called
A constant derived from the ideal gas equation
= 0.08206 L atm mol–1 K–1 or 8.314 L kPa mol–1 K–1.
A relation between the pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of a gas under conditions derived by combining the simple gas laws: Boyle's, Gay-Lussac's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws.
A solution in which the intermolecular forces between solute and solvent are equal to those in the separated components; the solution forms with no accompanying energy change.
Describes two substances, typically liquids, with negligible mutual solubility.

Matter (chemicals) present in a sample of matter that is mostly one type of chemical. For example, it is rare to find pure water, as it usually contains impurities (e.g., various elements, molecules of contaminants, carbon dioxide, and oxygen gas that's dissolved in the water).
The light that touches a surface.
A substance added to the sample in a titration analysis to permit visual detection of the end point.
An electrode that conducts electrons to and from the reactants in a half-cell but that is not itself oxidized or reduced.
Tendency of post-transition elements to act as if their valence s electrons are inert (i.e., to not participate in bonding).
A magnetic field where the magnetic strength, direction, or both, varies from point to point.
The instantaneous rate of a chemical reaction at
= 0 s (immediately after the reaction has begun).
Elements in the bottom two rows. Those in the first row are also called
, and those in the second row are also called
A chemical compound that has no carbon–hydrogen bonds.
Waves of the same frequency that are in alignment with each other (the peaks of both waves line up).
Rate of a chemical reaction at any instant in time, determined by the slope of the line tangential to a graph of concentration as a function of time.
Equation that relates the concentration of a reactant to the elapsed time of the reaction.
The difference used in telling one chemical apart from other chemicals depends only on what chemical it is and not on the amount of that chemical.
A property whose value depends only on the type of matter and not on the amount.
How different substances affect each other.
A process by which the waves combine to yield either an increase or a decrease in amplitude (intensity).
The sum of the radii of the positive and negative ions.
A species produced in one elementary step of a reaction and consumed in another step.
The various forces of attraction that may exist between the atoms and molecules of a molecular substance due to electrostatic phenomena.
The total of all kinds of kinetic and potential energies present in a substance or substances.

A set of seven base quantities and their units of measure: length is measured by meter, mass by kilogram, time by second, temperature by kelvin, electric current by ampere, amount of substance by mole, and luminous intensity by candela. Other units, such as centimeter and kilometer, are derived from the base units.
An empty space, or hole, in the regular array of atoms or ions in a crystal structure.
Forces within the molecule that keep the molecule together—the covalent bonds between the atoms.
As one variable increases, another variable decreases at the same rate, and vice versa.
An atom that has gained or lost electrons and therefore is electrically charged.
The electrostatic attraction between an ion and a molecule with a dipole.
A solvated anion and cation held together temporarily by moderate electrostatic attraction.
Electrostatic force of attraction between the oppositely charged ions of an ionic compound.
Chemical compound formed by positive and negative ion attraction.
Solids consisting of two or more kinds of ions that usually are of different sizes.
An estimate of the radius of an ion, determined from X-ray crystallography measurements on ionic solids.
A solid composed of positive and negative ions that are held together by electrostatic attractions.
The conversion of an atom or molecule into an ion through the gain or loss of one or more electrons.
An isomer in which a ligand has exchanged places with an anion or molecule that was originally outside the coordination sphere.
Amount of energy needed completely to remove an electron from its atom.
Subatomic particles or electromagnetic waves with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules, causing them to form ions.
The equilibrium constant for the autoionization of water.
Elements or compounds that crystallize with the same structure.
Describes two solutions whose concentration of solutes are identical on either side of a semipermeable membrane.
Atoms of the same element that have different masses due to different numbers of neutrons.
Describes a material with uniform properties in all directions.
SI unit of energy; 1 joule is the kinetic energy of an object with a mass of 2 kilograms moving with a velocity of 1 meter per second, 1 J = 1 kg m
Energy of a moving body, in joules, equal to 1/2 mv (where m = mass and v = velocity).
A model that describes the macroscopic behavior of gasses in terms of the microscopic motions of the atoms and molecules that comprise the gas.
